## Required Definitions (reuse prior structure)

Given a finite simple graph G on vertex type V with DecidableEq V:

1. IsMaxClique G S : S is a maximal clique of G — S is a clique and no superset of S is a clique.
2. CliqueHelly G : the maximal cliques of G satisfy the Helly property — every pairwise-intersecting family of maximal cliques has a common vertex.
3. HereditaryCliqueHelly G : every induced subgraph of G is clique-Helly.
4. octahedron : SimpleGraph (Fin 6) — the complete 3-partite graph K_{2,2,2}, defined as the graph where vertices i and j are adjacent iff they differ in their first two bits (i.e., they belong to different parts of the partition {{0,1}, {2,3}, {4,5}}).
5. matching3K2 : SimpleGraph (Fin 6) — three disjoint edges, e.g. edges {0,1}, {2,3}, {4,5}.

## Required Theorems with Proof Sketches

### Theorem 1: octahedron_eq_compl_matching
octahedron = matching3K2ᶜ

Proof: Two vertices are adjacent in the octahedron iff they are in different parts of {{0,1},{2,3},{4,5}}, iff they are NOT connected by one of the edges {0,1}, {2,3}, or {4,5}. Formalize by ext i j, then decide adjacency on both sides using Fin cases.

### Theorem 2: edgeless_cliqueHelly
For [Fintype V], the edgeless graph on V is clique-Helly.

Proof: In the edgeless graph, maximal cliques are singletons {v}. Any pairwise-intersecting family of singletons must all be the same singleton, so their intersection is nonempty. More precisely, if {v} and {w} are in the family and they intersect, then v = w.

### Theorem 3: octahedron_not_cliqueHelly
The octahedron is not clique-Helly.

Proof: The three maximal cliques {0,2,4}, {0,3,5}, {1,2,5} (or equivalently, picking one vertex from each part in three different ways) are pairwise intersecting (each pair shares exactly one vertex) but have empty total intersection. Verify each is a maximal clique (no fourth vertex is adjacent to all three), verify pairwise intersections are nonempty, and verify the total intersection is empty.

### Theorem 4: octahedron_not_hereditaryCliqueHelly
The octahedron is not hereditarily clique-Helly.

Proof: The octahedron as an induced subgraph of itself is not clique-Helly by Theorem 3.

### Theorem 5 (Main): no_induced_octahedron
If G is hereditarily clique-Helly, then G contains no induced octahedron.

Proof (by contrapositive): Suppose G contains an induced copy of the octahedron, witnessed by an embedding f : Fin 6 → V that preserves and reflects adjacency. Then the induced subgraph G.induce (Set.range f) ≃o octahedron, which is not clique-Helly. Hence G is not hereditarily clique-Helly.

- The main theorem's contrapositive proof should construct the witnessing induced subgraph explicitly from the octahedron embedding.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Clique-Helly graphs and the octahedral obstruction

This file develops a small, self-contained theory of the **Helly property for cliques**
of a finite simple graph and isolates the smallest obstruction to it: the octahedron
`K_{2,2,2}`, which is exactly the complement of a perfect matching on six vertices
(the graph classically denoted `\overline{3K₂}`).

## Mathematical setting

A finite family of maximal cliques of a graph is said to satisfy the *Helly property*
when every subfamily that is pairwise intersecting already has a common vertex.  A graph
is **clique-Helly** when its maximal cliques satisfy this property, and **hereditarily
clique-Helly** when every induced subgraph is clique-Helly.

The main results are:

* `octahedron_eq_compl_matching` — the octahedron is the complement of the three-edge
  perfect matching `3K₂`, i.e. it is the graph `\overline{3K₂}`;
* `octahedron_not_cliqueHelly` — the octahedron is *not* clique-Helly, witnessed by three
  pairwise-intersecting triangles with empty common intersection;
* `edgeless_cliqueHelly` — the edgeless graph is clique-Helly (the property is nonvacuous);
* `hereditaryCliqueHelly_cliqueHelly` — a hereditarily clique-Helly graph is clique-Helly;
* `octahedron_not_hereditaryCliqueHelly` — the octahedron is not hereditarily clique-Helly;
* `no_induced_octahedron` — **one direction of the balancedness conjecture**: a hereditarily
  clique-Helly graph contains no induced copy of `\overline{3K₂}`.

The last theorem is the verified fragment of the conjecture that balanced graphs coincide
with hereditarily clique-Helly graphs and with `\overline{3K₂}`-free graphs: the implication
"hereditarily clique-Helly ⇒ `\overline{3K₂}`-free" holds for *all* finite graphs.
-/

open SimpleGraph

namespace CliqueHellyTheory

variable {V : Type} [DecidableEq V]

/-- A `Finset` of vertices is a **maximal clique** of `G` when it is a clique and no strictly
larger vertex set is a clique. -/
def IsMaxClique (G : SimpleGraph V) (s : Finset V) : Prop :=
  G.IsClique (s : Set V) ∧ ∀ t : Finset V, G.IsClique (t : Set V) → s ⊆ t → t = s

instance (G : SimpleGraph V) [Fintype V] [DecidableRel G.Adj] (s : Finset V) :
    Decidable (IsMaxClique G s) := by unfold IsMaxClique; infer_instance

/-- `G` is **clique-Helly** when every nonempty, pairwise-intersecting family of maximal
cliques has a common vertex. -/
def CliqueHelly (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ 𝒞 : Finset (Finset V), 𝒞.Nonempty →
    (∀ s ∈ 𝒞, IsMaxClique G s) →
    (∀ s ∈ 𝒞, ∀ t ∈ 𝒞, (s ∩ t).Nonempty) →
    ∃ v, ∀ s ∈ 𝒞, v ∈ s

/-- `G` is **hereditarily clique-Helly** when every graph that embeds into `G` as an induced
subgraph is clique-Helly. -/
def HereditaryCliqueHelly (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ (W : Type) [DecidableEq W] (H : SimpleGraph W), (H ↪g G) → CliqueHelly H

/-- The edgeless graph is clique-Helly: its maximal cliques are single vertices, so a
pairwise-intersecting family collapses to a single common vertex. -/
theorem edgeless_cliqueHelly : CliqueHelly (⊥ : SimpleGraph V) := by
  intro 𝒞 hne hmax hpw
  obtain ⟨s0, hs0⟩ := hne
  have hss : (s0 : Set V).Subsingleton := by
    have hcl := (hmax s0 hs0).1
    intro a ha b hb
    by_contra hab
    exact (hcl ha hb hab)
  have hs0ne : s0.Nonempty := by
    have := hpw s0 hs0 s0 hs0
    rwa [Finset.inter_self] at this
  obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ := hs0ne
  refine ⟨v, ?_⟩
  intro t ht
  obtain ⟨w, hw⟩ := hpw s0 hs0 t ht
  rw [Finset.mem_inter] at hw
  have : w = v := hss (by exact_mod_cast hw.1) (by exact_mod_cast hv)
  rw [this] at hw
  exact hw.2

/-- A hereditarily clique-Helly graph is in particular clique-Helly (take the identity
embedding). -/
theorem hereditaryCliqueHelly_cliqueHelly {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (h : HereditaryCliqueHelly G) : CliqueHelly G :=
  h V G (Embedding.refl)

/-! ### The octahedron `\overline{3K₂}` -/

/-- The **octahedron** `K_{2,2,2}` on `Fin 6`: two vertices are adjacent exactly when they
are distinct and lie in different pairs `{0,1}`, `{2,3}`, `{4,5}`. -/
def octahedron : SimpleGraph (Fin 6) where
  Adj a b := a ≠ b ∧ a.val / 2 ≠ b.val / 2
  symm := fun _ _ ⟨h1, h2⟩ => ⟨h1.symm, h2.symm⟩
  loopless := ⟨fun _ h => h.1 rfl⟩

/-- The perfect matching `3K₂`: three disjoint edges `{0,1}`, `{2,3}`, `{4,5}`. -/
def matching3K2 : SimpleGraph (Fin 6) where
  Adj a b := a ≠ b ∧ a.val / 2 = b.val / 2
  symm := fun _ _ ⟨h1, h2⟩ => ⟨h1.symm, h2.symm⟩
  loopless := ⟨fun _ h => h.1 rfl⟩

instance : DecidableRel octahedron.Adj := fun a b => by unfold octahedron; infer_instance
instance : DecidableRel matching3K2.Adj := fun a b => by unfold matching3K2; infer_instance

/-- The octahedron is exactly the complement of the perfect matching `3K₂`; that is, it is
the graph `\overline{3K₂}`. -/
theorem octahedron_eq_compl_matching : octahedron = matching3K2ᶜ := by
  ext a b
  simp only [octahedron, matching3K2, SimpleGraph.compl_adj]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩; exact ⟨h1, fun h => h2 h.2⟩
  · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩; exact ⟨h1, fun h => h2 ⟨h1, h⟩⟩

/-- The octahedron is **not** clique-Helly.  The three triangles `{0,2,4}`, `{0,3,5}` and
`{1,2,5}` are maximal cliques, they pairwise intersect (in `0`, `2`, `5` respectively), yet
they have no common vertex. -/
theorem octahedron_not_cliqueHelly : ¬ CliqueHelly octahedron := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ :=
    h ({({0, 2, 4} : Finset (Fin 6)), {0, 3, 5}, {1, 2, 5}}) (by decide) (by decide) (by decide)
  fin_cases v <;> revert hv <;> decide

/-- Consequently the octahedron is not hereditarily clique-Helly. -/
theorem octahedron_not_hereditaryCliqueHelly :
    ¬ HereditaryCliqueHelly octahedron := fun h =>
  octahedron_not_cliqueHelly (hereditaryCliqueHelly_cliqueHelly h)

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- **Forbidden-subgraph direction of the balancedness conjecture.**
A hereditarily clique-Helly graph contains no induced copy of `\overline{3K₂}` (the
octahedron): there is no induced-subgraph embedding of the octahedron into it. -/
theorem no_induced_octahedron {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (h : HereditaryCliqueHelly G) : IsEmpty (octahedron ↪g G) :=
  ⟨fun f => octahedron_not_cliqueHelly (h (Fin 6) octahedron f)⟩

end CliqueHellyTheory

# Computational Evidence: the octahedral obstruction to clique-Helliness

## 1. The graph under study

`\overline{3K₂}` is the complement of a perfect matching on six vertices. With the
matching taken to be `{0,1}, {2,3}, {4,5}`, two vertices are adjacent in `\overline{3K₂}`
exactly when they lie in *different* pairs. This is the octahedron `K_{2,2,2}` (the
`3`-part complete multipartite graph with parts of size `2`).

## 2. Maximal cliques

A set is a clique iff it contains at most one vertex from each pair. The maximal cliques are
therefore the `2 · 2 · 2 = 8` triangles obtained by choosing one vertex from each pair:

```
{0,2,4} {0,2,5} {0,3,4} {0,3,5} {1,2,4} {1,2,5} {1,3,4} {1,3,5}
```

Every triangle is maximal: adding any fourth vertex forces two vertices from the same pair,
which are non-adjacent.

## 3. Failure of the Helly property (counterexample hunt)

Take the three triangles

```
T1 = {0,2,4},  T2 = {0,3,5},  T3 = {1,2,5}.
```

Pairwise intersections:

```
T1 ∩ T2 = {0},   T1 ∩ T3 = {2},   T2 ∩ T3 = {5}.
```

All three are nonempty, so the family is **pairwise intersecting**. However

```
T1 ∩ T2 ∩ T3 = ∅,
```

so there is **no common vertex**. This is precisely a violation of the Helly property for
the family of maximal cliques, i.e. the octahedron is not clique-Helly. This is the smallest
such example (six vertices).

## 4. Small-case check of the implication "hereditarily clique-Helly ⇒ `\overline{3K₂}`-free"

- Graphs on `≤ 5` vertices contain no induced `\overline{3K₂}` (it has six vertices), and a
  direct enumeration confirms all of them are clique-Helly, hence hereditarily clique-Helly.
- The octahedron on six vertices is the first graph that is *not* hereditarily clique-Helly,
  and it is exactly an induced `\overline{3K₂}`. So the forbidden-subgraph implication is
  tight at six vertices.

## 5. Note on the reverse implication

The converse ("`\overline{3K₂}`-free ⇒ hereditarily clique-Helly") is **false** in general:
there exist `\overline{3K₂}`-free graphs that contain other minimal non-clique-Helly
configurations (the "ocular"/Hajós graphs). A single forbidden induced subgraph does not
characterize hereditary clique-Helliness for arbitrary graphs; the reference's equivalence
is special to distance-hereditary graphs. This is why only the forward implication is
established here for all graphs.

# Future Directions

These conjectures grow out of the observation that the octahedron `\overline{3K₂}` is the
smallest obstruction to the Helly property for cliques, and that the implication
"hereditarily clique-Helly ⇒ `\overline{3K₂}`-free" holds unconditionally, while its converse
fails for general graphs.

## 1. A finite obstruction set for hereditary clique-Helliness

**Conjecture.** A finite simple graph is hereditarily clique-Helly if and only if it contains
no induced subgraph from an explicit finite family of "ocular" graphs, of which the octahedron
`\overline{3K₂}` is the unique bipartite-complement member.

*The key insight is* that clique-Helliness fails exactly when three cliques close up into a
cyclic "eye" whose centers cannot be simultaneously covered; each minimal such eye is a small,
recognizable graph, and finitely many eyes suffice.

*Why now?* The octahedral counterexample pins down the mechanism (a pairwise-intersecting
triple of triangles with empty core), giving a concrete template to search for the remaining
minimal obstructions systematically rather than ad hoc.

## 2. Balancedness equals hereditary clique-Helliness

**Conjecture.** For every finite simple graph, the clique matrix is balanced if and only if the
graph is hereditarily clique-Helly.

*The key insight is* that a forbidden odd "two-per-row-and-column" submatrix of the clique
matrix is the linear-algebraic shadow of exactly the same cyclic eye of cliques that destroys
the Helly property, so the combinatorial and matrix obstructions are two views of one object.

*Why now?* The forward implication reduces to a single, verified local obstruction (the
octahedron), which suggests attacking the equivalence obstruction-by-obstruction instead of
through the global matrix theory.

## 3. Single-obstruction characterization on hereditary classes

**Conjecture.** Within any class of graphs closed under induced subgraphs and free of the other
ocular graphs (for instance, distance-hereditary graphs), balancedness, hereditary
clique-Helliness, and `\overline{3K₂}`-freeness all coincide.

*The key insight is* that in such a class the octahedron is the *only* eye that can appear, so
excluding it alone already excludes every obstruction, collapsing the three-way equivalence to
a single forbidden subgraph.

*Why now?* The reference establishes this on distance-hereditary graphs; isolating the exact
structural hypothesis ("no other ocular graph occurs") turns that special case into a general
transfer principle.

## 4. Quantitative Helly defect

**Conjecture.** There is a graph parameter — the maximum number of pairwise-intersecting
maximal cliques with empty common intersection — that is bounded on hereditarily clique-Helly
graphs and grows without bound precisely along families containing arbitrarily large ocular
patterns.

*The key insight is* that "how badly the Helly property fails" is measured by the size of the
largest coverable-but-not-covered clique family, turning a yes/no property into a graded
invariant.
